title: Would You Mind If I Took It to the Beach?
scene: A friend offers to lend you her film camera for a harbor walk. You ask whether you can take it to the beach afterward. She sets a boundary about sand, and you agree on a way to return it safely.
sceneJa: 友人が港の散歩用にフィルムカメラを貸してくれることになった。ついでに海辺へ持って行ってもよいか尋ねると、砂が心配だと言われる。気まずくならずに相手の希望を尊重し、返却方法を決める。

chunks.en: A friend offered to lend me
chunks.ja: 友人が貸してくれると言ってくれた
彼女のフィルムカメラを

chunks.en: for a walk around the harbor.
chunks.ja: 港の周りを散歩するときに

chunks.en: I asked, 'Would you mind if I brought it
chunks.ja: 「それを持って行っても大丈夫かな」と尋ねた
彼女は「できれば持って行かないでほしいな」と言った
砂ってどこにでも入り込むし
特に古いカメラにはね、と
僕は「そりゃそうだね」と答えた

chunks.en: I'll bring it back to your place
chunks.ja: 君の家に返しに行くよ

chunks.en: before I go to the beach.'

chunks.ja: 「それなら大丈夫」と彼女は言い
僕にお礼を言ってくれた
先に確認したことに対して

chunks.en: I checked when she'd be home
chunks.ja: 何時ごろ家にいるか確かめた

chunks.en: so I could hand it back in person.
chunks.ja: 直接手渡しで返せるように

questions.question: Which split keeps the polite permission request together as a useful speaking unit?
options: Would you / mind if I brought / it to the beach afterward?
Would you mind if I brought it / to the beach afterward?
Would you mind / if I brought it to / the beach afterward?
questions.explanation: 'Would you mind if I brought it ...?' asks permission politely. The past form 'brought' refers to a possible future action here. Keep the request together before adding the destination.

questions.question: What does 'I'd rather you didn't' mean in this situation?
options: She would prefer that the camera not go to the beach.
She has decided not to lend the camera at all.
She wants to go to the beach instead of the harbor.
questions.explanation: The friend is setting a specific boundary: the camera should not be taken to the sandy beach. 'I'd rather you didn't' expresses a preference about someone else's action.

questions.question: What is the speaker doing by saying 'Fair enough'?
options: Acknowledging that the friend's concern is reasonable and accepting the limit.
Agreeing to take the camera to the beach secretly.
Telling the friend that her camera is too old to use.
questions.explanation: 'Fair enough' accepts the reason without arguing. The speaker then offers a concrete return plan, showing respect for the lender's preference.

speak: Imagine: a friend offers to lend you something valuable, but you want to use it in a different place. Read: read all six sentences, changing your tone for each speaker. Chunk: keep 'Would you mind if I brought it ...?', 'I'd rather you didn't', and 'Fair enough' together. Understand: 'Would you mind if I + past verb' politely asks permission; 'I'd rather you didn't' is a polite but clear preference, not a statement about the past. Check: answer the three questions. Speak: for 30 seconds, ask permission to use a borrowed item somewhere, respond to a reasonable boundary, and propose a practical alternative. Try 'Would you mind if I ...?', 'I'd rather you didn't', and 'Fair enough'. Final Read: read all six English sentences smoothly without Japanese, with a calm, respectful tone.
review: New: 'Would you mind if I ...?' (〜しても差し支えない？), 'I'd rather you didn't' (できれば〜しないでほしい), 'Fair enough' (なるほど、それなら分かる). Reuse Lesson 95 'That works for me' (それなら大丈夫) to accept a camera return plan instead of a café suggestion; Lesson 92 'Just to make sure' (念のため) to check a safe handover instead of a meeting entrance. Different from recent invitations and mix-ups: this story teaches asking permission, respecting a boundary, and offering an alternative. Usage cross-checked: https://dictionary.cambridge.org/us/grammar/british-grammar/mind and https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/would-rather-would-sooner .
